title: Regression & Classification

character.name: The Line Bender
character.tagline: Give me points, I'll give you a line. Give me classes, I'll draw a border.

oneLiner: The two bread-and-butter supervised tasks: predicting numbers (regression) and predicting categories (classification).
analogy: Regression is the fortune teller who predicts a NUMBER: 'This house will sell for $412,000.' Classification is the bouncer who predicts a CATEGORY: 'You're on the list' vs 'not tonight.' The Line Bender's simplest trick is drawing a straight line through data (linear regression) or drawing a boundary that separates groups (logistic regression / decision trees). Fancy models exist, but many real wins come from these humble tools done well.
objectives: Tell regression (predict a quantity) apart from classification (predict a category).
Understand linear and logistic regression at an intuitive level.
Know decision trees and k-nearest-neighbors as approachable classifiers.
Match a business problem to the right task type.
keyConcepts: Regression predicts continuous numbers (price, temperature, demand).
Linear regression fits a straight-line relationship; logistic regression outputs a probability for a class despite the name.
Decision trees split data with yes/no questions; they're interpretable but can overfit.
k-Nearest-Neighbors classifies a point by the majority vote of its closest neighbors.
Start simple: a well-tuned simple model is often competitive and easier to trust.

keyTerms.plain: Predicting a number on a sliding scale.
A classifier that outputs a probability (the name is a historical prank).
A flowchart of yes/no questions that ends in an answer.
You are who your nearest neighbors are — majority vote wins.

scenarios.scenario: A team wants to predict the exact number of units a product will sell next month.
scenarios.question: Which task type is this?
scenarios.explanation: Predicting a numeric amount (units sold) is regression. If instead they wanted 'will it sell out: yes/no,' that would be classification.

quiz.question: Predicting whether an email is spam or not spam is an example of:
quiz.explanation: Spam vs not-spam is a discrete category, so it's classification. Predicting a number would be regression.

quiz.question: Despite its name, logistic regression is used for:
options: Classification — it outputs a probability for a class
quiz.answer: Classification — it outputs a probability for a class
quiz.explanation: Logistic regression outputs a probability between 0 and 1 for class membership, making it a classifier.

quiz.question: A key weakness of a single deep decision tree is that it:
options: Tends to overfit, memorizing the training data
quiz.answer: Tends to overfit, memorizing the training data
quiz.explanation: Deep trees can fit noise. Ensembles like random forests and gradient boosting reduce this while keeping much of the power.

quiz.question: How does k-Nearest-Neighbors classify a new point?
options: By majority vote of its nearest labeled neighbors
quiz.answer: By majority vote of its nearest labeled neighbors
quiz.explanation: kNN looks at the k closest training points and takes the majority label — simple and intuitive, though slower at prediction time on large datasets.

quiz.question: Which task predicts a continuous value?
quiz.explanation: Regression outputs continuous numbers (e.g. price, temperature), while classification outputs discrete categories.
